---
title: "Component 5 — Power & Hitting"
---

Five products: **Statcast Smash**, **Moonshot Meter**, **Barrel Zone**,
**Launch Angle Rainbow**, and **Clutch Contact**.

## Measuring a batted ball

Three quantities come straight from the ball's flight after contact.

| measurement | how |
|---|---|
| **Exit velocity** | high percentile of instantaneous 3-D ball speed in the 400 ms after contact |
| **Launch angle** | the initial velocity vector over the first ~150 ms |
| **Carry** | distance from home at the ball's **first bounce**, not its maximum distance |

::: {.callout-important}
## Why carry uses the first bounce

The obvious approach — the ball's furthest point from home during the play — is
wrong, and it inflated our first leaderboard to a 503-foot "home run". Relay
throws move the ball further from home *after* it lands. Measuring at the first
recorded bounce (or the point where a descending ball returns to contact height)
dropped the season maximum to a believable 466.9 ft, with a 99th percentile of
411.7 ft.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset}

### R

```{r}
#| label: r-batted
#| eval: false
source("../R/R03_tracking_features.R")

ball  <- get_ball_track("y1_d122_IOL_VAS", 246)
ev    <- get_events("y1_d122_IOL_VAS", 246)
t_hit <- event_time(ev, EVENT[["HIT_INTO_PLAY"]])

exit_velocity(ball, t_hit)
launch_angle(ball, t_hit)
carry_distance(ball, t_hit)
```

### Python

```{python}
#| label: py-batted
#| eval: false
from components import c03_tracking_features as c03
c03.batted_ball_measures(game, play=246)
```

:::

## Statcast Smash

Ranked by **90th-percentile** exit velocity rather than the single hardest ball,
so the leaderboard rewards repeatable damage.

::: {.panel-tabset}

### R

```{r}
#| label: r-smash
#| eval: false
source("../R/R05_power_hitting.R")
statcast_smash(hits, lineups, min_balls = 5, top = 10)
```

### Python

```{python}
#| label: py-smash
#| eval: false
from components import c05_power_hitting as c05
c05.statcast_smash(tabs["hits"], lu, top=10)
```

:::

| player | max EV | 90th-pct EV | balls |
|---|---|---|---|
| NYN-2545 | 121.8 | **121.6** | 7 |
| JGO-5337 | 121.7 | 121.5 | 5 |
| VNG-5259 | 121.8 | 121.1 | 8 |
| ADQ-3824 | **122.0** | 119.4 | 14 |

## Barrel Zone

A *barrel* is the sweet-spot combination: exit velocity ≥ 95 mph with a launch
angle between 20° and 35°.

::: {.panel-tabset}

### R

```{r}
#| label: r-barrel
#| eval: false
barrel_zone(hits, lineups, min_balls = 8, top = 10)
plot_barrel_zone(hits)
```

### Python

```{python}
#| label: py-barrel
#| eval: false
c05.barrel_zone(tabs["hits"], lu, top=10)
```

:::

| player | barrels | balls | barrel rate |
|---|---|---|---|
| ARN-8132 | 18 | 177 | 10.2 % |
| PHD-2671 | 16 | 120 | **13.3 %** |
| ANI-3725 | 15 | 132 | 11.4 % |

## Launch Angle Rainbow

The visual that explains *why* launch angle matters: the same exit velocity
produces a groundout at 5° and a home run at 28°.

::: {.panel-tabset}

### R

```{r}
#| label: r-rainbow
#| eval: false
rainbow <- launch_angle_rainbow(hits, lineups, player = "ANI-3725")
rainbow$summary
plot_launch_rainbow(rainbow)
```

### Python

```{python}
#| label: py-rainbow
#| eval: false
data, summary = c05.launch_angle_rainbow(tabs["hits"], lu, player="ANI-3725")
summary
```

:::

Batted balls are bucketed the way broadcasters describe them — ground ball
(< 10°), line drive (10–25°), fly ball (25–50°), pop up (> 50°).

## Clutch Contact

Exit velocity is only half the story; *when* it happened is the other half. This
weights contact quality by the leverage of the moment:

$$\text{clutch contact} = \frac{EV}{100}\times\sqrt{LI}$$

::: {.panel-tabset}

### R

```{r}
#| label: r-clutch
#| eval: false
clutch_contact(pbp, top = 10)
```

### Python

```{python}
#| label: py-clutch
#| eval: false
c05.clutch_contact(enriched, top=10)
```

:::

The square root keeps a single enormous-leverage plate appearance from dwarfing
everything else on the leaderboard — the same compression used by the Clutch
Score in Component 2.
